items.stem: A public health nurse teaches a community group about tuberculosis. For each statement, select Accurate or Not accurate.

rows.text: Latent TB infection (LTBI) means the person has M. tuberculosis but is not ill and cannot transmit TB to others
Active pulmonary TB disease can be contagious and is spread by airborne droplet nuclei from cough or similar respiratory force
Everyone with a positive TB skin or blood test is highly contagious and must be placed in airborne isolation indefinitely without further evaluation
Active TB disease may cause cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and other symptoms and requires treatment

rationales.R1: Accurate. Merck: LTBI is asymptomatic and not infectious. OpenStax: LTBI — no symptoms; cannot transmit the bacteria.
rationales.R2: Accurate. Merck: TB is transmitted almost exclusively by inhalation of airborne particles (droplet nuclei) from people with active pulmonary TB. OpenStax: active TB is highly contagious via airborne transmission.
rationales.R3: Not accurate. A positive test indicates infection but further evaluation distinguishes LTBI from active disease; LTBI is not contagious (Merck; OpenStax).
rationales.R4: Accurate. Merck and OpenStax list cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss among active TB symptoms; active disease requires treatment.

items.stem: An older adult in Ontario arrives with unexplained bruises in several stages of healing and appears fearful when the caregiver answers for them. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Interview the older adult alone (at least for part of the encounter) with private, direct questions about safety and possible mistreatment. In Ontario, immediately report suspected abuse of a long-term care or retirement-home resident; do not assume a universal duty to report community-dwelling older adults to adult protective services.
Allow only the caregiver to provide the entire history and never speak with the older adult privately.
Ignore bruising because all older adults bruise easily and never document findings.
Confront the caregiver angrily in front of the client and refuse any further assessment.

rationales.A: Correct. Interview the older adult alone and ask directly about mistreatment. Merck describes referral to Adult Protective Services, which reflects common US duties and is not Ontario law for older adults living in the community. Ontario’s Fixing Long-Term Care Act, 2021, s. 28, requires an immediate report to the Director when a long-term care resident is abused or neglected with harm or risk of harm, and a parallel duty applies in retirement homes. Do not rely only on the caregiver’s history.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck warns caregiver reluctance to leave the older adult alone with a clinician is concerning; private interview is essential.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Unexplained injuries and inconsistent histories are red flags requiring assessment and documentation (Merck).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Confronting the caregiver in front of the client can escalate risk. Assess privately, then follow the Ontario reporting duty that applies to the setting rather than a universal adult-protective-services mandate.

items.stem: A client at 30 weeks gestation is in preterm labour. Complete the teaching/plan: Antenatal {B1} are given primarily to promote {B2}, and short-term tocolysis may be used mainly to {B3}.

ngn.template: A client at 30 weeks gestation is in preterm labour. Complete the teaching/plan: Antenatal {B1} are given primarily to promote {B2}, and short-term tocolysis may be used mainly to {B3}.

B2.text: fetal lung maturity / reduce neonatal respiratory distress risk
elective induction at 28 weeks without indication

B3.text: gain time (often ~48 hours) for corticosteroids to take effect before birth
replace the need for any neonatal resuscitation planning
guarantee delivery will never occur preterm

rationales.B1a: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: antenatal corticosteroids are standard when preterm birth is anticipated in the eligible gestational window.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Vitamin C is not the antenatal therapy that accelerates fetal lung maturity in preterm labour.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Antitussives are unrelated to fetal lung maturation.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Topical antifungals do not promote fetal surfactant/lung maturity.
rationales.B2a: Correct. OpenStax: corticosteroids promote fetal lung maturity/surfactant and reduce RDS risk; Merck: corticosteroids given in the preterm window for fetal benefit.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Not a fetal lung indication.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Goal is fetal maturation, not elective early induction.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Unrelated to antenatal corticosteroid purpose.
rationales.B3a: Correct. Merck: tocolytics can usually delay labour for at least 48 hours so corticosteroids can be given.
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. Tocolysis does not eliminate need for neonatal preparedness.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Tocolysis does not permanently prevent preterm birth.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Monitoring continues; tocolysis is time-limited bridge therapy.

items.stem: A client on postpartum day 2 after cesarean birth has fever, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Notify the provider and anticipate ordered broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
Monitor vital signs and assess for worsening infection or early sepsis cues
Document uterine tenderness, lochia characteristics, and fever trend
Reassure that fever and foul lochia after cesarean never require evaluation
Withhold all assessment of the fundus and discharge home without follow-up teaching
Teach the client to report increasing pain, rising fever, or worsening foul discharge

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: treatment is broad-spectrum antibiotics; OpenStax: nurse administers ordered antibiotics for endometritis.
rationales.B: Correct. OpenStax: monitor for worsening infection/sepsis; Merck notes potential progression to severe infection.
rationales.C: Correct. Both sources describe fever, uterine tenderness, and abnormal/foul discharge as key findings to track.
rationales.D: Incorrect. These findings indicate postpartum endometritis needing prompt evaluation/treatment (Merck; OpenStax).
rationales.E: Incorrect. Assessment and teaching are required; endometritis can progress (OpenStax).
rationales.F: Correct. OpenStax discharge teaching includes contacting the provider for worsening infection signs.

items.stem: A young adult with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, Kussmaul respirations, glucose markedly elevated, and anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Complete the bowtie: priority condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) with hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis

actions.text: Initiate ordered IV fluid volume resuscitation and continuous IV insulin per protocol
Monitor and replace potassium as ordered while insulin/fluids are given
Withhold all fluids and insulin because hyperglycemia is always self-limited
Discharge home immediately without laboratory follow-up
Encourage unsupervised intense exercise before treatment

parameters.text: Blood glucose trend and resolution of acidosis/ketosis
Serum potassium and cardiac/neurologic status during insulin and fluid therapy

rationales.K1: Correct. Merck/OpenStax: DKA features hyperglycemia with ketonemia/acidosis; clinical picture matches.
rationales.K2: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not explain ketoacidosis.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Client has marked hyperglycemia and acidosis.
rationales.A1: Correct. Merck: volume expansion and insulin replacement; OpenStax: aggressive IV fluids and IV insulin.
rationales.A2: Correct. Merck: prevent hypokalemia; OpenStax: monitor/correct potassium especially during treatment.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. DKA requires prompt fluids and insulin (both sources).
rationales.A4: Incorrect. DKA is an ICU/emergency condition needing monitored therapy.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Exercise is not initial DKA management.
rationales.P1: Correct. Therapy is titrated to glucose and clearing of ketoacidosis (both sources).
rationales.P2: Correct. Potassium shifts with insulin; both sources emphasize potassium monitoring.
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Not a DKA monitoring parameter.

items.stem: A client with bulimia nervosa who induces vomiting after binge episodes reports palpitations. Which nursing priority is most appropriate?

options.text: Obtain ordered electrolyte laboratory studies (especially potassium), monitor cardiac status, and support supervised nutrition/anti-purging interventions while notifying the provider of concerning findings.
Encourage unsupervised intense laxative use after every meal.
Ignore palpitations because electrolyte imbalance never occurs in bulimia.
Withhold all vital signs and laboratory monitoring permanently.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: serious electrolyte disturbances, especially hypokalemia, can occur; measure electrolytes. OpenStax: hypokalemia and arrhythmia risk; interventions include labs, electrolyte replacement, and interrupting purging.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Laxative misuse worsens fluid/electrolyte imbalance (both sources describe purging harms).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hypokalemia is a recognized complication (Merck; OpenStax).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Monitoring labs and cardiac status is essential (OpenStax care plan).

items.stem: A client suddenly develops intense fear with palpitations, shortness of breath, and a sense of doom. Immediate ECG and medical evaluation have ruled out acute coronary syndrome and other life-threatening medical causes. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate during the panic attack?

options.text: Remain calm, move the client to a quieter less stimulating environment if possible, coach slow deep breathing, and offer brief reassurance that the attack will pass while continuing to monitor.
Crowd the client with loud multiple conversations and argue that the fear is imaginary.
Leave the client completely alone without observation in an unsafe isolated area.
Force the client to sprint immediately to 'burn off' the attack without assessment.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: nurse remains calm, encourages slow deep breathing, offers reassurance, and uses a quiet calm environment. Merck: after medical causes are considered/excluded, panic attacks themselves are not medically dangerous; supportive care and psychotherapy approaches are used.
rationales.B: Incorrect. OpenStax advises reducing stimuli and remaining calm, not escalating sensory load or arguing.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Supportive presence and monitoring are indicated during intense symptoms (OpenStax).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Intense exercise is not the immediate panic-attack nursing intervention described in the sources.

verification_log.checks: Merck: hypothermia core ≤35°C; mild (32–35°C) passive rewarming with heated blankets and warm fluids. OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: hypothermia when temperature <95°F (35°C); OpenStax Fundamentals: dress appropriately / remove cold exposure risk for hypothermia prevention—treatment concordance via Merck passive rewarming + OpenStax definition

items.stem: An older adult found outdoors has a measured core temperature of 33.5°C, is shivering, and has intact circulation without cardiovascular instability. Which intervention best matches initial management of mild hypothermia?

options.text: Begin passive rewarming: move to a warm environment, apply insulating/heated blankets, and provide warm oral fluids if the client can safely swallow, while monitoring core temperature and perfusion.
Leave wet cold clothing on and keep the client in a drafty unheated area.
Apply ice packs to the trunk to further lower core temperature.
Withhold all temperature monitoring because shivering always means normal temperature.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: mild hypothermia (about 32–35°C) with intact thermoregulation is treated with passive rewarming (warm environment, heated blankets, warm fluids). OpenStax Clinical Skills defines hypothermia as core temperature <35°C (95°F), matching this presentation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck/OpenStax emphasize removing cold exposure and supporting rewarming, not continued heat loss.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Core temperature guides severity and treatment (Merck Key Points).

items.stem: A 3-year-old with nonsevere acute otitis media is mildly ill, afebrile to low-grade fever only, and has reliable caregiver follow-up. Which teaching point is most accurate?

options.text: Provide appropriate analgesia (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed) for ear pain, and understand that selected nonsevere cases may be observed for about 24–48 hours with planned reassessment, starting antibiotics if symptoms worsen or fail to improve.
Never treat pain because analgesics are never used in ear infections.
Immediate IV vancomycin is required for every mild earache without examination.
Ignore fever ≥39°C with severe systemic illness because observation is always mandatory.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: analgesia for all children with AOM; observation is an option for selected nonsevere cases with follow-up. CPS Caring for Kids: acetaminophen/ibuprofen for pain; watchful waiting 24–48 hours when illness is not severe, with antibiotics if no improvement or worsening.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sources emphasize treating pain.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Not first-line for uncomplicated nonsevere AOM (Merck prefers oral amoxicillin when antibiotics are indicated).
rationales.D: Incorrect. High fever/severe illness warrants prompt antimicrobials (CPS; Merck).

items.stem: A term newborn develops visible jaundice at 18 hours of life. Which interpretation and action is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat as potentially pathologic jaundice: notify the provider promptly, obtain ordered bilirubin evaluation, and prepare for indicated therapy (often phototherapy) based on level and risk.
Assume all jaundice before 24 hours is always harmless physiologic jaundice requiring no evaluation.
Discharge without assessment because early jaundice never needs follow-up.

rationales.C: Incorrect. Early-onset jaundice requires prompt evaluation (both sources).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Not the treatment pathway for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
